summary: A complete tree forces breadth-first search to inspect every internal node before reaching its first leaf, which is linear in the tree size. The queue traversal matches that bound and can stop at the first leaf.

optimality.argument: In a complete n-node tree whose leaves all occupy the deepest level, every internal node must be ruled out before the first leaf can be identified. There are Theta(n) internal nodes, so the worst-case time is Omega(n). The current BFS enqueues and dequeues each visited node once and never processes a node after finding the first leaf, for O(n) worst-case time and O(w) queue space.

replacement_checks.evidence: A complete tree has Theta(n) internal nodes at shallower depths, all of which precede every leaf in breadth-first order.
Each visited node enters and leaves the deque once, and the algorithm returns immediately upon removing the first true leaf.

The source-fidelity-verified examples and note cover a shallow leaf, a one-sided chain, and the exact leaf definition; black-box real-test execution verifies every existing ordinary check without inspecting its definition.
